title: Automating Large Scale Refactors with Parallel Agents - Robert Brennan, OpenHands
talk_summary: Robert Brennan describes OpenHands orchestration for large refactors: decompose work into PR-sized batches, run parallel agents in isolated sandboxes, and use verifier/fixer loops with human review. He emphasizes dependency ordering, shared context via reviewed files, and limiting concurrency to what humans can review.

takeaways.what_they_do: Build a file dependency graph, group semantically related files into batches, and process leaf batches first so each agent gets a PR-sized unit.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we can simply use the existing directory structure to make sure that semantically related files appear inside the same batch.
takeaways.numbers: 380 files / 60k lines in core agent; PR-sized batches; couple hundred lines changed

takeaways.what_they_do: A verifier checks each batch against tests/rules; failures spawn a fixer agent with tools, then verification reruns before human merge.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Use the verify to identify problems. Use the fixer to spin up the address those problems. Review and merge those PRs.
takeaways.numbers: 30x improvement on CVE time resolution cited

takeaways.what_they_do: Create a compatibility layer so old and new systems coexist, migrate components in parallel, validate each component, then remove scaffolding.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we basically had an agent set up uh some scaffolding that would allow us to to work with both Redux Redux and Zustan at the same time.

takeaways.what_they_do: Agents write learned constraints to a shared markdown/micro-agent file via PR, with human review to prevent noise, instead of broadcasting all context.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can allow the agents to actually modify this file themselves. Uh maybe they send a pull request into the file as they learn new things.

takeaways.what_they_do: Start with 3-5 concurrent agents when one human reviews; scale to hundreds/thousands only by routing PRs to individual teams rather than one reviewer.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I would suggest limiting yourself to about three to five concurrent agents. Uh I find more than that your brain starts to break.
takeaways.numbers: 3-5 concurrent agents; hundreds/thousands at scale; ~90% automation

takeaways.what_they_do: Run each agent in its own Docker/Kubernetes workspace so it can execute commands autonomously without risking the host.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if it's got its own like containerized environment somewhere in the cloud, you can run a little bit more safely
takeaways.numbers: thousands of CVEs could run on Kubernetes
